ideas.title: Vortex Trap: Escape the Turbulence
ideas.paper: 2605.24901v1 — Geometry, elasticity, and activity in the transport of self-propelled filaments in turbulence
ideas.pitch: The paper's actual punchline is counterintuitive: activity does NOT generically help a self-propelled elastic filament escape turbulent vortices. If propulsion is coupled to the filament's own shape, it stays diffusive and gets trapped; only fixed-direction propulsion (independent of the filament's bent/curled state) lets it superdiffuse across vortex structures, and low Weissenberg-number elasticity actually strengthens the trapping by cooperating with activity to keep the filament extended. Build a single-file canvas demo: render a 2D 'turbulent' flow as a sum of randomly seeded, decaying point vortices (classic method, no real Navier-Stokes solve needed), drop in a chain-of-springs filament with a propulsion force, and give the user three sliders — activity strength, elasticity (Weissenberg number), and a toggle between 'shape-coupled propulsion' vs 'fixed-direction propulsion.' Track and plot mean-squared displacement live so the user watches the trajectory go from diffusive (trapped, looping in one vortex) to superdiffusive (skipping across vortices) purely by flipping the propulsion-coupling toggle — literally feeling the paper's core, surprising result with their own hands.

ideas.title: Nodal Line Casino: Watch Berry's Cancellation Happen
ideas.paper: 2607.09946v1 — Statistics on Yau's conjecture: Variance asymptotics
ideas.pitch: The paper proves sharper variance bounds for the nodal volume (zero-set length) of random Riemannian waves and shows 'Berry's cancellation' — the variance of nodal length collapses far faster than naive fluctuation estimates would suggest, especially on manifolds without conjugate points / negatively curved ones — as frequency (spectral window) grows. Build a canvas demo: generate random monochromatic waves as a sum of N random-phase plane waves at a fixed wavenumber k on a flat torus (trivial to compute on a grid), extract the nodal set with marching squares, and compute nodal curve length. Run many independent random-wave samples at a given k, live-update a running variance-of-nodal-length histogram, then let the user drag a slider to increase k and watch the variance visibly shrink relative to naive sqrt-scaling — a direct, hands-on feel for a genuinely deep result in random wave / Yau's conjecture research, no backend, just per-frame JS math.

ideas.title: PathogenID Cloud — zero-shot MALDI-TOF pathogen ID across hospitals
ideas.paper: 2608.08182v1 — Biologically Informed Representation Learning for Robust Cross-Center Generalization of MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry (DALMA)
ideas.pitch: The paper's actual result: DALMA, by baking biological structure into the representation (not just statistical domain-alignment tricks), gets state-of-the-art zero-shot microbial ID on two held-out clinical centers it never trained on, plus antimicrobial-resistance prediction and reliable 'I don't know' selective-prediction via latent novelty detection — validated across 7 datasets, 3 countries. That zero-site-tuning property is the actual product gap in clinical microbiology: every hospital lab currently has to locally recalibrate its MALDI-TOF classifier because instrument/reagent drift breaks transfer. A startup wrapping this into a hosted inference API — hospital uploads a raw spectrum, gets back species ID + AMR risk + a calibrated confidence/novelty flag, zero local retraining — is a real wedge into hospital microbiology labs and reference labs in underserved regions that can't afford a data-science team to keep recalibrating models. Land-and-expand: start with AMR flagging (higher willingness to pay, life-or-death timing pressure) then broaden to full species ID.

ideas.title: SentimentRAG Signal Desk
ideas.paper: 2310.04027v2 — Enhancing Financial Sentiment Analysis via Retrieval Augmented Large Language Models
ideas.pitch: The paper's concrete claim is a 15-48% accuracy/F1 jump over ChatGPT/LLaMA-style zero-shot sentiment on financial text, achieved by (1) instruction-tuning an LLM specifically to output sentiment labels instead of free text, and (2) retrieving similar historical financial-news snippets as grounding context before the model answers — directly targeting the sparse/context-poor nature of terse financial headlines. Buildable as a small self-contained project (not single-HTML, but a weekend-scale tool): pull a rolling window of headlines for a ticker list, embed + store them in a local vector index, and for each new headline retrieve the k most similar historical headlines (with their realized next-day price move as weak labels) as in-context examples before asking an LLM for a sentiment score. Log predicted sentiment vs actual next-day return to build a live calibration/backtest dashboard — a legitimate small research tool for probing whether retrieval-augmented sentiment actually adds trading-signal value out of sample, directly testing the paper's claim on your own data rather than taking it on faith.

ideas.title: Character Detector: break the L-function symmetry
ideas.paper: 2607.00332 [math.NT] Functional Equations Characterize Dirichlet Characters
ideas.pitch: The paper's converse theorem says the functional equation Λ(s)=εΛ(1-s) for a Dirichlet series ∑f(n)n^-s forces f to be a primitive Dirichlet character (no multiplicativity assumption needed). Build a single-page toy: pick or hand-draw a coefficient function f(n) (start from a real character mod q, e.g. Legendre symbol), plot the completed L-function's values along the critical line and its reflection at 1-s side by side on an Argand-style canvas. A slider lets you perturb individual f(n) away from character values; as you do, the two sides visibly stop mirroring each other. Watching the symmetry snap when you break the one algebraic constraint the paper isolates is a genuinely rare way to *feel* a converse theorem.

ideas.title: Sparse Matrix Query Race: peel vs naive
ideas.paper: 2606.12179 [cs.DS] Nearly Instance Optimal Sparse Matrix Approximation from Matrix-Vector Products
ideas.pitch: The paper shows query complexity for recovering a matrix with known sparsity pattern S from matrix-vector products is governed by degen(S) — the smallest k such that iteratively stripping all rows/cols with ≤k nonzeros empties the matrix — with Õ(degen(S)) achievable and Ω(degen(S)) necessary. Build a grid where the user draws a sparsity pattern (diagonal, banded, arrowhead, random bipartite graph) and watches two bars race: a naive one-query-per-column baseline vs. an animated 'peel' process that strips low-degree rows/cols round by round exactly as the paper's algorithm does, ticking off the query count as it goes. Makes an abstract instance-optimality bound into a literal countdown you can race against different shapes.

ideas.title: Outrage vs Reality: the social amplification phase transition
ideas.paper: 2603.29282 [physics.soc-ph] Social Amplification Dominates Collective Hazard Response
ideas.pitch: The paper fits a compact hazard+contagion model to COVID-era US state data and finds social influence outweighed direct hazard forcing in over 80% of states, with a critical coupling strength beyond which response stops tracking real risk and runs away on negativity bias. Build a two-line chart: a stylized 'ground truth hazard' curve and a 'collective stress' curve computed from the paper's coupled hazard+contagion update rule, with one slider for social-coupling strength. Below the transition point the stress line hugs the hazard line; crank the slider past it and stress visibly decouples and overshoots, reproducing the paper's core finding as something you can trigger with your own hand. Extremely shareable given everyone's lived through a real version of this curve.

ideas.title: Narrative Drift: a divergence score for hype vs fundamentals
ideas.paper: 2603.29282 [physics.soc-ph] Social Amplification Dominates Collective Hazard Response
ideas.pitch: Productize the paper's hazard-vs-contagion decomposition as a general-purpose 'narrative drift' score: feed it any pair of a ground-truth signal (case counts, injury reports, box scores, earnings) and a social-chatter signal (X/Reddit sentiment volume), fit the same coupled model, and flag when the public narrative has decoupled from the fundamentals the paper's math says drives runaway response. Direct fit for the sports-betting/trading instincts already in play (fade public overreaction lines before the market corrects) and for crisis-comms teams wanting an early warning that pile-on is diverging from actual severity.

ideas.title: Permutation Snap: Watch Gradient Ascent Find the Only Maxima
ideas.paper: 2607.12431v2 - Local Maxima of the Entrywise l4 Norm on the Orthogonal Group
ideas.pitch: The paper proves that when you maximize sum(entry^4) over the orthogonal group, the ONLY local (hence global) maximizers are signed permutation matrices - every other stationary point has an explicit escape direction. Build a single-page demo: for SO(2), plot the objective f(theta)=cos^4+sin^4+... as you rotate a 2x2/3x3 orthogonal matrix around a slider, showing it has exactly 4 (or 8, 24...) sharp peaks precisely at the axis-aligned rotations. Then run live gradient ascent from a random starting rotation and animate the matrix heatmap 'snapping' toward a permutation matrix (all 0s and ±1s) while a trajectory dot climbs the landscape curve. Bonus panel: apply the exact same gradient ascent to un-mix two blindly combined sine/audio waveforms (classic ICA-via-kurtosis setup) and let the user hear the mixed signal 'de-scramble' into two clean tones as the rotation converges to a permutation - this is literally the real-world reason this theorem matters (why ICA optimization landscapes have no bad local optima).

ideas.title: Instant Noise: Brownian-Bridge Differential Privacy Timeline
ideas.paper: 2606.11760v1 - A Fast Gaussian Mechanism under Continual Observation, with Applications
ideas.pitch: The paper's trick: instead of the classic O(log T) binary-tree mechanism for releasing a running noisy count under continual observation, they show any single noise value in the tree can be sampled in O(1) time using Brownian bridge conditioning (sample the endpoints, then condition midpoints on them recursively/implicitly), preserving identical correlation structure. Build a demo with a 1000-step timeline slider; clicking any point instantly reveals its DP-noised cumulative count. A toggle mode shows the 'naive' way materializing the whole log-depth tree path (with visible per-node computation flashing, artificially slowed) versus the 'fast' way resolving instantly via bridge conditioning - same output distribution, dramatically different work. A live histogram overlay proves the two modes are statistically indistinguishable across many re-runs, which is the actual selling point of the paper.

ideas.title: StatGate: statistics-first pre-filter for SFT/RLHF data buyers
ideas.paper: 2607.18960v1 - SFGA: A Statistics-First Gating Architecture with Adjudicative Escalation for Trustworthy SFT Data Procurement
ideas.pitch: SFGA scores candidate training data on diversity/utility/redundancy with confidence intervals, auto-accepting/rejecting when intervals are tight and only escalating ambiguous batches to an LLM-debate adjudicator - hitting 0.90 gate accuracy / 0.83 F1 at $0.017/unit, versus an always-escalate baseline at $0.020, while landing between an always-verify baseline (0.75) and an oracle (0.98). The paper also flags that the LLM-debate step itself is biased (80% con-side win rate, 52% position-flip rate under advocate swap) - i.e. today's 'LLM judge' data-curation tools are quietly unreliable. Pitch: a drop-in pre-purchase/pre-training data gate for labs buying or scraping SFT/RLHF corpora, sold on 'cheap statistical triage first, expensive adjudication only when genuinely uncertain, and audited adjudicators so you're not fooled by debate-order bias.' Wedge: publish a benchmark showing how much current vendors' LLM-judge filters flip under trivial reordering.

ideas.title: The Orchids That Are Winning Right Now - And Losing By 2070
ideas.paper: 2511.01122v1 - The Future Orchid Diversity of Great Britain and Ireland using an SDM Approach
ideas.pitch: The paper's twist is counterintuitive and visual: species distribution models projecting to 2050/2070 under climate + land-use change scenarios show significant losses in orchid richness across most of GB and Ireland - including in Ireland, where historical trend data shows orchids currently GAINING ground. Some species are projected toward local extinction by 2070. A explainer video builds the hook around 'the flowers doing best today are the ones the models say are already doomed' - walk through why SDMs diverge from naive trend extrapolation (1km-grid climate + dynamic land-use vs. simple historical counts), animate a toy version of a species range contracting on a stylized UK/Ireland grid as a 'warming' slider increases, and end on the conservation-policy implication: don't read current upward trends as safety.

ideas.title: Numerical Semigroup Tree Explorer (the 'unreachable score' game)
ideas.paper: 2607.23111v1 [math.CO] Algorithms and results on multiparameter counting of numerical semigroups
ideas.pitch: The paper proves an exact formula for the number of numerical semigroups with a given genus, Frobenius number, AND multiplicity simultaneously (for m >= (F+1)/3), and grows the 'tree of numerical semigroups' via a seeds/pruning algorithm to compute previously-unknown counts (n78-n80) and tables up to F=128. Build a single-HTML canvas demo that frames this as a game: pick a set of 'move values' (like darts, or a video-game combo scoring system), and watch the semigroup tree branch live as you increase genus, with the Frobenius number highlighted as 'the largest score you can never make.' A live counter shows the running total of semigroups matching the paper's exact multiparameter formula, so you can literally watch the theorem being verified node-by-node. Nice fit for the math->games whimsy angle -- it's the Chicken McNugget problem with a real recent theorem behind it.

ideas.title: Docking Synergy Viewer: two plant compounds vs two cancer drugs
ideas.paper: 2505.08632v1 [q-bio.BM] Computational Analysis using Multi-ligand Simultaneous Docking of Withaferin A and Garcinol Reveals Enhanced BCL-2 and AKT-1 Inhibition
ideas.pitch: The paper's headline numbers are concrete and dramatic: multi-ligand simultaneous docking (MLSD) of withaferin A + garcinol together scores -11.88 kcal/mol against BCL-2 (beating venetoclax's -9.73) and -13.74 kcal/mol against AKT-1 (crushing melatonin's -7.24), implying real synergy from combining the two natural compounds. Build a single-HTML page embedding 3Dmol.js (CDN, no build step) to load the real BCL-2 and AKT-1 PDB structures, spin/zoom the binding pockets, and pair the 3D view with an interactive bar chart toggling between 'single ligand' and 'MLSD combo' affinities against the commercial-drug baselines. Makes the 'natural compound combo beats a real chemo drug' claim something you can rotate and stare at, not just a number in an abstract.

ideas.title: GLID-lite: a depth-fingerprint deepfake checker that runs in your browser
ideas.paper: 2607.18770v1 [cs.CR] GLID: Gated Local Intrinsic Dimension Repairs the Blind Spots of Face-Forgery Detectors
ideas.pitch: GLID's actual finding is oddly specific and very visual: forged faces bend a frozen ViT's token manifold at generator-family-specific depths -- GAN artifacts spike the local intrinsic dimension at the LAST layer, diffusion artifacts spike it MID-network -- and gating on this 12-D depth signal alone (no retraining) hits 0.805 mean AUC across 16 unseen-generator axes while cutting run-to-run variance 5.5x. Build a client-side-only tool using transformers.js (CDN) to run a small ViT on an uploaded photo, estimate local intrinsic dimension per layer (a lightweight k-NN/TwoNN estimator, tractable in plain JS), and plot the depth-vs-LID curve live -- if it spikes late, flag 'GAN-like'; if it spikes mid-network, flag 'diffusion-like.' Topical (deepfakes), and it turns an abstract geometric claim into a chart anyone can read.

ideas.title: Teacher Envelope Sandbox: watch a student beat every one of its teachers
ideas.paper: 2608.03610v2 [cs.CL] Language-Specialized Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Multilingual LLM-Based ASR
ideas.pitch: The paper's most counterintuitive claim: after training separate language-specialized ASR teachers by RL and distilling them into one multilingual student via language routing + token-level distillation, the student 'surpasses the empirical performance envelope defined by the best-performing RL teachers on nearly all benchmarks' -- i.e. it beats not just the average teacher, but the BEST teacher in each teacher's own specialty. Build a synthetic 2D playground (canvas/d3, no libraries needed): scatter points in 3-4 colored 'language' regions, spawn one overfit 'specialist' classifier per region (each great locally, bad elsewhere), then compute a routed+blended 'student' decision boundary and shade where the student's accuracy exceeds the max of ALL specialists pointwise. Let users drag region boundaries and noise level and watch the envelope-beating effect appear or collapse -- makes a genuinely surprising ML result about distillation something you can poke at in 30 seconds.

ideas.title: Contamination Breakpoint
ideas.paper: 2607.02681 — Contaminated Multi-task Learning with Heterogeneity: Fundamental Limits and Optimal Algorithms
ideas.pitch: The paper proves naive multi-task estimators (regularization/outlier-detection) suffer contamination error that scales as ε√d/n — it gets WORSE as feature dimension d grows — while their filtering-based robust gradient descent hits the dimension-free optimal rate ε/√n. Build a single-page toy: simulate K linear-regression tasks in d dimensions, corrupt an ε-fraction of tasks with adversarial gradients, and run 'naive averaging' vs 'robust filtering' side by side. Sliders for d, ε, n drive two live error curves on a canvas chart — crank d up and watch the naive line rocket upward while the robust line stays flat. That's the paper's whole theorem, felt in your hands in under a minute.

ideas.title: Squeeze the Channel
ideas.paper: 2605.18531 — Enhanced Ionic Conductivity of confined Ionic-Liquid in Angstrom-scale 2D channels
ideas.pitch: The result is a sharp, nonmonotonic peak: ionic-liquid conductivity in a van-der-Waals slit channel hits 26.7 S/m (>30x bulk) at exactly 1.02 nm channel height, driven by ion-pair breakup increasing free-ion density — but squeeze further to 0.68 nm and steric hindrance craters conductivity below bulk. A co-solvent (acetonitrile) pushes the peak to ~145 S/m. Build a canvas toy: a 2D slit with animated +/- ion particles and a height slider from 2nm down to 0.6nm. At wide/loose heights ions clump into slow pairs; at the 1.02nm sweet spot they visibly break apart and zip through fast; squeeze past that and they jam. A live conductivity gauge traces the same nonmonotonic curve from the paper, with a 'co-solvent' toggle that blows the peak up further.

ideas.title: Feedback Router
ideas.paper: 2608.09109 — Different Feedback, Different Updates: Selective Self-Learning from User Interactions for LLMs (SLIFT)
ideas.pitch: SLIFT's core move: classify each piece of user feedback as Fix (broad requirement, updates a shared 'Generalist' LoRA adapter via feedback-conditioned self-distillation), Spec (narrow, condition-specific, updates a 'Specialist' adapter as a residual), or Null (no reliable update direction — model stays frozen). Build a toy where a model is a point in a 2D weight-space plot with two adapter vectors (Generalist, Specialist). Feed it canned feedback snippets tagged Fix/Spec/Null (or auto-tag via a simple keyword heuristic) — watch only the relevant adapter vector nudge on Fix/Spec, and nothing move at all on Null. Makes the paper's central claim — 'not all feedback deserves the same gradient' — visually undeniable in a way the abstract can't.

ideas.title: ESG Weight Reveal
ideas.paper: 2312.00202v2 — Investigate The ESG Score Methodology
ideas.pitch: The paper's whole question is whether Refinitiv's aggregation of 10 category scores (Emissions, Resource Use, Innovation, Workforce, Human Rights, Community, Product Responsibility, Management, Shareholders, CSR Strategy) into one overall ESG number is a reliable, statistically justified methodology — or an arbitrary weighting choice dressed up as a measurement. Build an interactive leaderboard: sample companies with their 10 category sub-scores, default weights matching Refinitiv's published scheme, and sliders per category. Drag a weight and watch company rankings visibly reshuffle in real time — a direct, felt demonstration of how much of 'your ESG score' is actually a policy choice. As a wedge, pitch this as a due-diligence tool for asset managers/analysts who need to stress-test a target's ESG rating under alternative, defensible weighting schemes before trusting it in a screen.

ideas.title: Rank-Width Playground: Pivot Your Way Past the Forbidden 25
ideas.paper: 2607.23101v2 — The Excluded Vertex-Minors and Pivot-Minors for Rank-Width at Most Two
ideas.pitch: The paper computer-searched >9x10^10 graphs to find the complete list of forbidden substructures for rank-width ≤2: exactly 25 excluded vertex-minors (8-10 vertices) and 609 excluded pivot-minors (8-12 vertices) — any graph avoiding all of them provably has rank-width ≤2. Build a single-page graph editor (canvas + adjacency matrix) where you draw a graph up to ~12 nodes and apply local complementation / vertex-deletion (vertex-minor moves) or edge-pivot operations live. Compute rank-width exactly and instantly by brute-forcing GF(2) matrix rank over all 2^n vertex bipartitions (trivial at n≤12) and show a running badge: 'rank-width = 2, still safe' vs 'rank-width jumped to 3 — you just created a forbidden substructure.' This makes an abstract linear-algebra graph invariant something you can feel by dragging edges around, and it's 100% client-side JS/canvas — no data files needed, the whole theorem is computable from scratch.

ideas.title: Blind Transcription Duel
ideas.paper: 2608.03617v1 — Machine-readable catalogue of the Tsiolkovsky papers + handwriting-readability metric
ideas.pitch: The paper's clever trick: measure handwritten-text-recognition accuracy WITHOUT ground truth, by comparing two independent readings of the same page and using their agreement rate as a proxy for difficulty (median 37% word agreement across 294 real manuscript/typescript pairs, validated at 0.92 rank-correlation to true accuracy). Turn this into an interactive toy: render a passage in a cursive canvas font, then simulate two 'independent noisy readers' by randomly dropping/smudging different characters per copy at a difficulty you control with a slider. Show live word-agreement percentage between the two noisy transcriptions and plot how it tracks true accuracy as difficulty rises — reproducing the paper's central empirical claim (agreement-without-ground-truth is a valid accuracy proxy) as something you can literally drag a slider and watch happen. No image assets needed since the 'noise' is synthetic; can add a real Tsiolkovsky archive scan later for flavor.

ideas.title: Ground-Truth-Free HTR Scorer (open-source lib)
ideas.paper: 2608.03617v1 — Machine-readable catalogue of the Tsiolkovsky papers + handwriting-readability metric
ideas.pitch: Generalize the paper's core methodological contribution — estimating OCR/HTR accuracy from agreement between two independent transcriptions of the same document, rather than requiring expensive ground-truth transcripts — into a small reusable library/CLI. Archives and digitization projects (libraries, historical societies, genealogy sites) constantly need to know 'is this handwriting recognizer good enough to trust' without paying for gold-standard transcription. Feed it two transcript files (e.g. two different OCR engines, or two human transcribers) of the same pages and it outputs the paper's agreement-based accuracy estimate plus a confidence interval, directly operationalizing their validated result (unbiased to within 1 percentage point, rank correlation 0.92 vs published editions). Very buildable: it's just tokenization + word-alignment + agreement statistics, no ML training required.

ideas.title: Peptide Stiffness Atlas
ideas.paper: 2505.08850v1 — High-throughput Screening of the Mechanical Properties of Peptide Assemblies
ideas.pitch: The paper computes Young's modulus for every possible di- and tripeptide sequence via high-throughput coarse-grained MD (validated against AFM), then trains an ML model to extend predictions across the full pentapeptide sequence space — mapping which amino-acid combos make stiff vs. soft self-assembled materials. Build an interactive 20x20 heatmap of all dipeptide combinations where hovering shows predicted Young's modulus, with a toggle to drill into tripeptide space and a 'stiffest combos' leaderboard — letting a viewer literally see the sequence-to-stiffness landscape the paper is mining for next-gen biomaterials. Ideally seeded with the paper's own released dataset/supplement (if public) for real numbers; as a fallback, seed with a physically-motivated toy scoring function (hydrophobicity + aromatic stacking proxies) clearly labeled as illustrative until real data is swapped in.

ideas.title: Construct Miner: LLM-Powered Survey Instrument Auditor
ideas.paper: 2602.02604v1 — AI Assisted Economics Measurement From Survey: Evidence from Public Employee Pension Choice
ideas.pitch: The paper's framework uses an LLM to 'soft-map' raw survey items onto latent economic constructs (e.g. separating beliefs from constraints in pension-choice behavior), aggregate into sub-dimension scores, and validate with overlap/redundancy diagnostics and out-of-sample testing — turning messy Likert-scale surveys into economically interpretable measurement. Package this as a SaaS for HR analytics teams, market researchers, and pollsters: upload a survey codebook + response CSV, get back an auto-discovered construct taxonomy, sub-scores per respondent, redundancy warnings ('these 4 items are measuring the same thing'), and a validation report — replacing the expensive psychometrician contract most mid-size orgs can't afford. MVP is buildable tonight as a single HTML page that posts the CSV + item text to an LLM API and renders the resulting construct map and scores client-side.
